New WordPress Pre-Auth XSS Could Lead to PHP Code Execution - Patch ASAP

The Hacker News
2026-08-07 11 use cases 4 techniques 5 kill-chain phases detected

WordPress has fixed a pre-authentication reflected cross-site scripting (XSS) flaw in its login screen that affects every version of the content management system. Under additional conditions, the bug can be chained into PHP code execution on the server. Tracked as&nbsp;CVE-2026-64638&nbsp;(CVSS score: 8.9), the High-severity vulnerability requires no attacker privileges. According to pwn.ai,

WordPress CVE-2026-64638 login-screen XSS payload in wp-login.php request AIDelivery Medium
Hunts inbound requests to wp-login.php whose username/query carries the parser-differential XSS signature described by pwn.ai: a tag opened with '<' immediately followed by whitespace (URL-encoded %3C%20 / %3C+ / %3C%09) so strip_tags() treats it as text but wp_kses_post() renders it as live DOM. This is the pre-auth initial-access step of the XSS2Shell chain. Rationale: Uses the article's exact parser-differential tell ('tag-like string containing whitespace after the opening <') expressed as its URL-encoded forms against the specific vulnerable endpoint wp-login.php; this is far tighter than a generic <script> XSS grep. Defender XDR ships no inbound web-access-log table so defender_kql is intentionally empty. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/WordPress/wordpress-develop/security/advisories/GHSA-52p2-r8wf-jcrf • https://securityonline.info/wordpress-security-update-7-0-3/ • https://wordpress.org/news/2026/08/wordpress-7-0-3-release/
ATT&CKT1190 T1059.007
Data sourcesWeb
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Automated vulnerability scanners (Nuclei, Burp, WPScan) firing XSS test payloads at wp-login.php
  • Legitimate redirect_to values that happen to contain encoded '< ' sequences
  • Bug-bounty researchers testing the site
  • Broken links where encoded HTML leaks into the login URL
  • Security-training/phishing-simulation platforms probing the login form
Suppression filter
| where HttpRequestHeaderUserAgent !has_any ("WPScan", "Nuclei", "Burp", "sqlmap", "nikto")
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull full Url and HttpRequestHeaderReferer for the hit; decode the payload and confirm it opens a tag with trailing whitespace (< script). Check whether the source IP later hits authorize-application.php or wp-json on the same host. 2) Contain: confirm WordPress core is >= 7.0.3 (or the 4.7+ backport); if not, patch immediately and force-logout active admin sessions. Block the source IP at the WAF. 3) Hunt: pivot on the same SrcIp/UserAgent for /wp-json/ JSONP+_envelope calls, application-password creation, and new plugin ZIP uploads to confirm chain progression.
ImWebSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where Url has "/wp-login.php"
| where Url has_any ("%3C%20", "%3C+", "%3C%09", "%3c%20", "%3c+")
| project TimeGenerated, SrcIpAddr, HttpHostName, HttpMethod, Url, HttpRequestHeaderReferer, HttpRequestHeaderUserAgent, HttpStatusCode
| order by TimeGenerated desc

WordPress REST JSONP + _envelope=1 401-wrapping abuse (XSS2Shell execution) AIExploitation High
Hunts requests to /wp-json/ REST endpoints that combine a JSONP callback with _envelope=1. pwn.ai's chain uses REST JSONP to run attacker JS in the site origin and _envelope=1 to wrap an anonymous 401 denial inside an outer HTTP 200 so jQuery still executes the body as script. The combination of both parameters on the REST origin is highly specific to this technique. Rationale: Both _jsonp and _envelope=1 on a wp-json request is the article's named evasion primitive; legitimate WordPress clients almost never request JSONP wrapped in an envelope, so requiring both parameters together yields a low-FP alert. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/WordPress/wordpress-develop/security/advisories/GHSA-52p2-r8wf-jcrf • https://securityonline.info/wordpress-security-update-7-0-3/
ATT&CKT1059.007 T1190
Data sourcesWeb
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legacy JavaScript widgets legitimately using REST JSONP callbacks
  • Uptime/monitoring probes that append envelope parameters
  • Developer testing of REST responses in a browser
  • Third-party integrations reading wp-json with _jsonp for cross-origin embeds
Suppression filter
| where SrcIpAddr !in ("127.0.0.1", "::1") and HttpHostName !startswith "staging"
Response runbook
1) Triage: capture the callback name and target REST route in Url; check HttpStatusCode (expect outer 200 wrapping an inner 401) and whether the same session/IP loaded wp-login.php with an XSS payload just before. 2) Contain: verify core >= 7.0.3; block the source IP; force-reauth admins. 3) Hunt: from the same SrcIp/session, look for authorize-application.php approvals with external success_url and subsequent plugin uploads to confirm escalation.
ImWebSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where Url has "/wp-json/"
| where Url has "_jsonp=" and Url has "_envelope=1"
| project TimeGenerated, SrcIpAddr, HttpHostName, HttpMethod, Url, HttpStatusCode, HttpRequestHeaderUserAgent
| order by TimeGenerated desc

WordPress Application Password approval redirected to external success_url AIInstallation High
Hunts requests to /wp-admin/authorize-application.php where the success_url points to a host different from the site itself. In the XSS2Shell chain the origin XSS drives the native Application Password approval control so WordPress mints an API credential and redirects it to an attacker-selected HTTPS success_url, avoiding theft of the admin's primary password. Rationale: Targets the article's exact credential-access mechanism (authorize-application.php minting a credential redirected to an attacker success_url) and reduces noise by only flagging when the success_url host differs from the site host, which is the malicious variant. Sigma omitted because the host-comparison is a computed cross-field check. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/WordPress/wordpress-develop/security/advisories/GHSA-52p2-r8wf-jcrf • https://patchstack.com/articles/wordpress-7-0-3-released-12-vulnerabilities-found-and-fixed/
ATT&CKT1098.001 T1212
Data sourcesWeb
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate third-party apps (mobile app, Jetpack, WooCommerce connectors) requesting Application Passwords with their own callback host
  • Developer registering an API integration with an external redirect
  • Password managers or SSO brokers on a different subdomain
  • Multisite setups where the callback host legitimately differs from the front-end host
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify which admin session approved the credential and the SuccessHost it was sent to; verify whether that app/host is a sanctioned integration. 2) Contain: in wp-admin > Users > Profile, revoke the newly created Application Password; force-reauth and rotate the admin's password; block SuccessHost egress. 3) Hunt: search for REST calls (Basic auth) from unfamiliar IPs/user-agents using the new credential, plugin-upload activity, and new administrator account creation immediately afterward.
ImWebSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where Url has "/authorize-application.php"
| where Url has "success_url="
| extend SuccessUrl = url_decode(extract(@"(?i)success_url=([^&]+)", 1, Url))
| extend SuccessHost = tostring(parse_url(SuccessUrl).Host)
| where isnotempty(SuccessHost) and SuccessHost != HttpHostName
| project TimeGenerated, SrcIpAddr, HttpHostName, Url, SuccessUrl, SuccessHost, HttpRequestHeaderUserAgent, HttpStatusCode
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats summariesonly=true count from datamodel=Web where Web.uri_path="*authorize-application.php*" AND Web.uri_query="*success_url=http*" by Web.src, Web.dest, Web.uri_path, Web.uri_query, Web.http_user_agent, Web.status | drop_dm_object_name(Web) | rex field=uri_query "success_url=(?<success_url>https?[^&]+)" | eval success_host=replace(success_url,"https?(?:%3A%2F%2F|://)([^%/&]+).*","\1") | where success_host!=dest | sort - count
| tstats summariesonly=false count from datamodel=Web where Web.uri_path="*authorize-application.php*" AND Web.uri_query="*success_url=http*" by Web.src, Web.dest, Web.uri_path, Web.uri_query, Web.http_user_agent, Web.status | drop_dm_object_name(Web) | rex field=uri_query "success_url=(?<success_url>https?[^&]+)" | eval success_host=replace(success_url,"https?(?:%3A%2F%2F|://)([^%/&]+).*","\1") | where success_host!=dest | sort - count
Malicious PHP file written under wp-content/plugins by web-server worker AIInstallation Medium
Hunts new .php files created under wp-content/plugins/ by the PHP/web-server worker process. In XSS2Shell the attacker uses the stolen Application Password to upload a ZIP that WordPress extracts into the plugins directory, planting an unactivated web shell that can be requested directly. Flags the file-drop persistence step on the host. Rationale: Anchors on the article's persistence step (ZIP extracted into wp-content/plugins, PHP requestable directly) and scopes to writes performed by the PHP/web worker, which is the malicious-upload path rather than an admin editing files on disk. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/WordPress/wordpress-develop/security/advisories/GHSA-52p2-r8wf-jcrf • https://securityonline.info/wordpress-security-update-7-0-3/
ATT&CKT1505.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate plugin installation/update via wp-admin or WP-CLI writing PHP files as the web user
  • Scheduled auto-updates of plugins
  • Composer/deploy pipelines that run as the web user
  • Backup/migration plugins restoring plugin files
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !in~ ("root") and InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has "wp-cli"
Response runbook
1) Triage: review the new .php file's contents for eval/base64/system() and check whether it belongs to a known plugin slug; correlate the write time with an authorize-application.php approval and a plugin-upload REST call. 2) Contain: quarantine/remove the file, disable direct PHP execution from plugin dirs, and rotate any Application Passwords and DB credentials in wp-config.php. 3) Hunt: look for direct HTTP GETs to the new .php path, php-fpm spawning shell commands, and creation of rogue admin accounts.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where FolderPath has "/wp-content/plugins/"
| where FileName endswith ".php"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName has_any ("php-fpm","php","httpd","apache2","nginx")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, FolderPath, FileName, ActionType, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where TargetFilePath has "/wp-content/plugins/"
| where TargetFileName endswith ".php"
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("php-fpm","php","httpd","apache2","nginx")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, ActorUsername
| order by TimeGenerated desc

WordPress PHP worker spawning OS shell (web-shell command execution) AIActions on Objectives High
Hunts php-fpm/apache/nginx worker processes spawning shells or network tools (sh, bash, curl, wget, python, perl, nc). This is the terminal impact stage of XSS2Shell where PHP is requested directly from the uploaded plugin and runs operating-system commands at the web worker's privilege level, exposing wp-config.php DB credentials and worker-readable secrets. Rationale: Targets the article's stated impact ('operating-system commands with that worker's privileges') via the high-signal LOLBin pair of a web/PHP worker parent spawning a shell/network tool child, which is almost never legitimate on a WordPress host. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/WordPress/wordpress-develop/security/advisories/GHSA-52p2-r8wf-jcrf • https://securityonline.info/wordpress-security-update-7-0-3/ • https://wordpress.org/news/2026/08/wordpress-7-0-3-release/
ATT&CKT1505.003 T1059.004
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Backup/migration plugins that shell out to mysqldump, tar, or rsync
  • Image-optimization plugins invoking imagemagick/exec via PHP
  • WP-Cron tasks launching curl/wget for scheduled fetches
  • SEO or CDN plugins calling external CLIs
  • Legitimate deploy hooks running as the web user
Suppression filter
| where ProcessCommandLine !has_any ("mysqldump", "wp-cron", "imagemagick", "convert ", "rsync")
Response runbook
1) Triage: capture ProcessCommandLine of the child (look for reverse-shell, wp-config.php reads, credential dumping) and identify the parent PHP path/plugin; confirm the plugin is not a sanctioned one. 2) Contain: kill the process tree, isolate the host, rotate wp-config.php DB credentials and all Application Passwords, and remove the malicious plugin directory. 3) Hunt: review outbound connections from the worker to attacker infrastructure, new administrator accounts (wp_users), file changes to posts/pages, and the preceding authorize-application.php / plugin-upload activity.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName has_any ("php-fpm","php","httpd","apache2","nginx")
| where FileName in~ ("sh","bash","dash","curl","wget","python","python3","perl","nc","ncat")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, FolderPath
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("php-fpm","php","httpd","apache2","nginx")
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("sh","bash","dash","curl","wget","python3","perl","nc","ncat")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ParentProcessName, ParentProcessCommandLine, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Growing Up The Hard Way

The Hacker News
2026-08-07 5 use cases 4 techniques 3 kill-chain phases detected

Open Source had a great childhood. For two decades it got to be a kid. It ran around barefoot, gave everything away, trusted strangers, and never once thought about who was watching. It ran the kind of lemonade stand that took IOUs from anyone who wandered up — take what you need, pay me back whenever, no need to leave a name. It was idyllic. It was also, in retrospect, a little feral. Then,

Actions on Objectives
—
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha) · Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key.
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage.
Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc

New NatJack Attacks Hijack TCP Sessions and Spoof DNS by Manipulating NAT Tables

The Hacker News
2026-08-07 7 use cases 3 techniques 3 kill-chain phases detected

Security researcher Malcolm Stagg has disclosed a new attack class called&nbsp;NatJack&nbsp;that manipulates network address translation (NAT) connection state to hijack active TCP sessions, spoof DNS responses, expose mapped ports, and exhaust NAT tables. Presented at Black Hat USA 2026, the research found affected behavior across independently developed implementations, including Windows and

Actions on Objectives
—
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration. → Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s)
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] Exposed hosts vulnerable to NatJack Windows NAT/Hyper-V origin-validation flaw (CVE-2026-56181) · [LLM] Exposed hosts vulnerable to NatJack Linux Netfilter conntrack SYN/RST teardown (CVE-2026-63913) · Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha)
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key.
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage.
Exposed hosts vulnerable to NatJack Windows NAT/Hyper-V origin-validation flaw (CVE-2026-56181) AIExploitation High
Surfaces Windows/Hyper-V hosts still exposed to the NatJack Windows NAT spoofing-from-adjacent-network flaw (CVE-2026-56181) so they can be prioritised for patching and untrusted-workload segmentation. Article-specific because it pins the exact CVE and the patched builds (24H2 26100.8875, 25H2 26200.8875, 26H1 28000.2525, Server 2025 26100.33158) rather than a generic NAT technique. Rationale: Pins the exact article CVE (CVE-2026-56181) and Microsoft's patched builds; TVM CveId is authoritative and avoids the ambiguous 26100-build revision math. No endpoint behavioural signal exists for the spoof itself because the NatJack forged response is NAT-rewritten to look like the legitimate peer. Cross-checked against: • https://www.networkworld.com/article/4206287/natjack-exploits-put-nat-security-assumptions-to-the-test-at-black-hat.html • https://www.synack.com/blog/malcolm-stagg-black-hat-2026/ • https://thehackernews.com/2026/08/new-natjack-attacks-hijack-tcp-sessions.html
ATT&CKT1557 T1040 T1498
Data sourcesVulnerabilities.Vulnerabilities
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • TVM inventory lag: host already updated to 26100.8875+/26200.8875+/28000.2525+/26100.33158+ but the vuln scan has not refreshed yet.
  • Hyper-V, WSL2, or Windows Sandbox not installed, so the vulnerable Windows NAT (winnat) driver is not loaded and the attack surface is absent.
  • Patch installed but pending reboot, so the running OSRevision still reports the pre-fix value.
  • Host sits on an isolated management VLAN with no untrusted workload sharing its NAT, so it is vulnerable-but-not-exploitable per the article's own precondition.
  • Gold/build-lab image flagged that never carries production traffic.
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm OSBuild/OSRevision is below the fixed level (24H2 26100.8875, 25H2 26200.8875, 26H1 28000.2525, Server 2025 26100.33158) and check whether Hyper-V/WSL2/Windows Sandbox NAT is actually enabled. 2) Contain: prioritise the KB rollout; where patching is delayed, move untrusted workloads off any NAT segment shared with the host and enable IP Source Guard on the access switch. 3) Hunt: enumerate other guests/hosts behind the same NAT, confirm internal traffic is encrypted (TLS), and review firewall/gateway logs for abnormal TCP RST/SYN bursts or DNS-response anomalies aimed at co-located hosts.

Exposed hosts vulnerable to NatJack Linux Netfilter conntrack SYN/RST teardown (CVE-2026-63913) AIExploitation High
Surfaces Linux hosts still on a kernel below the NatJack-fixed releases for the Netfilter conntrack direction-validation flaw (CVE-2026-63913), where a crafted SYN + invalid-sequence RST prematurely closes an active NAT conntrack entry. Article-specific because it targets the exact CVE and the fixed stable kernels (5.10.259, 5.15.210, 6.1.176, 6.6.143, 6.12.93, 6.18.35, 7.0.12, 7.1). Rationale: Pins the exact article CVE (CVE-2026-63913) and the kernel.org fixed stable releases; TVM CveId cleanly handles distro-backported version strings that a naive kernel-version compare would misjudge. The SYN-then-invalid-sequence-RST conntrack teardown is only observable in full packet capture / IDS, not in Defender/Sentinel/Falcon endpoint schemas, so exposure is the deployable pivot. Cross-checked against: • https://www.networkworld.com/article/4206287/natjack-exploits-put-nat-security-assumptions-to-the-test-at-black-hat.html • https://www.synack.com/blog/malcolm-stagg-black-hat-2026/ • https://thehackernews.com/2026/08/new-natjack-attacks-hijack-tcp-sessions.html
ATT&CKT1557 T1040 T1498
Data sourcesVulnerabilities.Vulnerabilities
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Running-vs-installed kernel mismatch: patched kernel is installed but the box has not rebooted, so the live kernel is still vulnerable (or the reverse false-positive after reboot).
  • Host does not use Netfilter NAT/conntrack (not a gateway, container host, or SNAT/DNAT router), so real exploitability is low.
  • Distro-backported kernels (RHEL/Ubuntu) whose version string looks older than the mainline fix but already contains the patch — scanner version-compare false positive.
  • Containers/network namespaces sharing one host kernel counted as multiple exposed assets.
  • Single-tenant NAT with no untrusted neighbour behind it, so the article's shared-NAT precondition is not met.
Response runbook
1) Triage: compare the running kernel (uname -r) against the fixed stable releases (5.10.259, 5.15.210, 6.1.176, 6.6.143, 6.12.93, 6.18.35, 7.0.12, 7.1) and confirm the host actually performs Netfilter NAT (iptables/nftables SNAT/DNAT or acts as a conntrack gateway). 2) Contain: schedule the kernel update + reboot; where delayed, separate untrusted workloads from the shared NAT and apply IP Source Guard. 3) Hunt: review firewall/conntrack and IDS logs for anomalous SYN followed by out-of-window RST against long-lived flows, and verify internal service traffic is TLS-encrypted so a hijacked conntrack entry yields no cleartext.

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha)
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → RMM tool installed by non-IT user — remote-access utility for hands-on-keyboard
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → OAuth consent / suspicious app grant
Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB

``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.

Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;

    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)

              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)

| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,

SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"

id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d01
status: experimental
description: |

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Malware Can Abuse Windows Hello for Business Keys for Persistent Entra ID Access

The Hacker News
2026-08-07 7 use cases 4 techniques 4 kill-chain phases detected

Entra ID researcher Dirk-jan Mollema demonstrated that malware already running in a signed-in Windows session can silently use the victim's Windows Hello for Business key to authenticate to Microsoft Entra ID. The attacker can then establish longer-term cloud access, register a device it controls, obtain a Primary Refresh Token (PRT), and add further authentication methods where tenant policies

title: Infostealer - Non-Browser Process Accessing Browser Credential Stores
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d01
status: experimental
description: |
    Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies
    SQLite databases from Chrome/Edge/Firefox profile directories. Any

references:

author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02

logsource:

detection:

level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"

        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent

| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"

   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"

Claude Code and Gemini CLI Flaws Let a GitHub Issue Reach CI Workflow Secrets

The Hacker News
2026-08-07 10 use cases 3 techniques 6 kill-chain phases detected

A GitHub issue opened by an account with no repository privileges was enough to execute code on the CI runners behind Anthropic's and Google's own coding-agent repositories. On OpenAI's, it was enough to hijack the next agent run. Novee Security ran the attack against each vendor's agent in the configuration that the vendor ships by default, and presented the work at Black Hat USA on August 5.

CVEsCVE-2026-12537 CVE-2026-54316
ATT&CKT1190 T1566 T1566.002

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration. → Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s)
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] Gemini CLI OS command injection via crafted .gemini/.env (CVE-2026-12537) · Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] Claude Code validator bypass: git push --receive-pack command injection · Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha)
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] ChainDrop persistence: Claude Code SessionStart hook / VS Code folderOpen task drop · [LLM] Codex second-pass hijack: AGENTS.md written inside a CI checkout
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] Claude Code API-key exfil via Hugging Face download-counter (CVE-2026-54316)
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage.
Claude Code validator bypass: git push --receive-pack command injection AIExploitation Medium
Hunts git invocations carrying a populated --receive-pack= flag value, the exact primitive Novee used to smuggle a payload past Claude Code's single-quote-stripping command validator so it reached the CI runner. In agent/CI contexts a custom receive-pack path is almost never legitimate and any shell metacharacters in it are attacker-controlled. Rationale: Uses the article's exact abused flag `git push --receive-pack` (a flag git executes) whose value was the injection sink after Claude Code stripped single-quoted text. A populated `--receive-pack=` in an agent/CI process tree is high-fidelity and rare in benign use. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/08/claude-code-and-gemini-cli-flaws-let.html
ATT&CKT1059.004 T1211
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Git server admins invoking a custom receive-pack binary (e.g. gitolite/gerrit tooling)
  • Developers mirroring repos to a self-hosted git that requires an explicit receive-pack path
  • CI jobs that legitimately set --receive-pack for a non-standard git host
  • Internal tooling wrapping git push with a hardened receive-pack shim
Suppression filter
| where not(ProcessCommandLine has_any ("gitolite","gerrit") and InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("sshd","perl","perl.exe"))
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Pull the full ProcessCommandLine and decode the --receive-pack= value; confirm whether it contains shell metacharacters ($(), ;, |, backticks) rather than a plain path, and identify the parent (node/claude/gemini). Step 2 (contain): If the value is a command payload, isolate the runner/host, revoke any tokens exposed to that job, and freeze the triggering workflow. Step 3 (hunt): Pivot on the same DeviceName for outbound egress to huggingface.co or attacker infra and for writes to AGENTS.md/.claude/.vscode configs in the checkout.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName in~ ("git.exe","git")
| where ProcessCommandLine has "--receive-pack="
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, ProcessCommandLine, FolderPath
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where ActingProcessName has "git"
| where ActingProcessCommandLine has "--receive-pack="
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ParentProcessName, ParentProcessCommandLine, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: git push --receive-pack Command-Value Injection
id: 8f2b1c4a-6d3e-4a71-9c02-1e5f7a9b0c31
description: Detects git invoked with a populated --receive-pack= flag value, the primitive used to bypass Claude Code's command validator and reach a CI runner (CVE-less Novee finding).
references:
  - https://thehackernews.com/2026/08/claude-code-and-gemini-cli-flaws-let.html
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/08/07
tags:
  - attack.t1059.004
  - attack.t1211
logsource:
  category: process_creation
detection:
  selection:
    Image|endswith:
      - '/git'
      - '\git.exe'
    CommandLine|contains: '--receive-pack='
  condition: selection
falsepositives:
  - Advanced git server administration specifying a custom receive-pack binary path
level: high
source:linux.auditd @auditd.type:EXECVE @process.name:git @process.command_line:*--receive-pack\=*
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 ImageFileName=/git(\.exe)?$/i
| regex("--receive-pack=", field=CommandLine)
| table([aid, ComputerName, UserName, ParentBaseFileName, CommandLine])
ENDPOINT

Claude Code API-key exfil via Hugging Face download-counter (CVE-2026-54316) AICommand & Control Medium
Hunts a Claude Code (node) process making an abnormally high, sustained volume of requests to huggingface.co, the covert channel CVE-2026-54316 abused to leak an API key one character at a time via the public download counter. Normal agent use touches HF sparsely; a per-character leak generates a burst of sequential requests. Rationale: Anchors on the article's named exfil channel (Hugging Face public download counter, CVE-2026-54316, char-by-char leak) plus the Claude Code/node initiating process. Volume-to-HF-from-agent is the observable signature since content itself is a single benign-looking counter fetch. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/08/claude-code-and-gemini-cli-flaws-let.html

| where not(InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("huggingface_hub","transformers","datasets","resolve/main"))
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Confirm the initiating process is Claude Code/node and inspect the request paths — a real model pull hits resolve/blob URLs, a leak repeatedly hits download-count/API endpoints with tiny responses. Correlate against Claude Code version (<2.1.163 is vulnerable). Step 2 (contain): Rotate any ANTHROPIC/API keys reachable by that context and block egress from the runner pending review. Step 3 (hunt): Check the same host for untrusted content ingested into the Claude Code context (issue text, cloned repo files) and for git --receive-pack injection or AGENTS.md tampering.

Gemini CLI OS command injection via crafted .gemini/.env (CVE-2026-12537) AIDelivery High
Hunts creation of a .gemini/.env file, the crafted input that reaches Gemini CLI's container launcher and yields OS command injection on the CI host before the sandbox starts (CVE-2026-12537, CVSS 10.0). The file appearing inside a checkout — especially written by git during clone — is the delivery artifact. Rationale: Uses the article's exact crafted path `.gemini/.env` named as the CVE-2026-12537 injection vector. A .env under .gemini appearing inside a repo checkout (particularly written by git) is a narrow, high-signal artifact of the delivery step. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/08/claude-code-and-gemini-cli-flaws-let.html
ATT&CKT1059.004 T1554 T1211
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem

  • Repo template that ships a sample .gemini/.env for onboarding
  • Dotfile-sync tooling restoring a user's Gemini config
  • CI setup step creating a benign .gemini/.env from a secret store
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("git","git.exe","curl","wget") or InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("clone","checkout")
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Read the .gemini/.env contents and the initiating process — flag any shell metacharacters or command substitution in values, and note whether git (clone/checkout) wrote it, meaning it arrived from an untrusted repo. Confirm Gemini CLI version (<0.39.1 / run-gemini-cli <0.1.22 is vulnerable). Step 2 (contain): Halt the runner before the Gemini launcher executes, quarantine the file, and rotate host/CI credentials reachable pre-sandbox. Step 3 (hunt): Look on the same host for a shell/child spawned by the Gemini/node launcher and for tool-allowlist bypass behaviour (--yolo auto-approved commands).

ChainDrop persistence: Claude Code SessionStart hook / VS Code folderOpen task drop AIInstallation Medium
Hunts repository-planted autorun artifacts reported by Pillar Security for the ChainDrop npm worm: a Claude Code SessionStart hook in .claude settings and a VS Code folderOpen task in .vscode/tasks.json, which fire when a developer opens the workspace rather than on install. Focuses on these files being written into a checkout by git/clone. Rationale: Grounded in the article's Pillar Security reference to ChainDrop planting a Claude Code SessionStart hook and a VS Code folderOpen task (firing on workspace open, not install). Scoping the write initiator to git/npm/clone separates repo-delivered autoruns from a developer's own IDE config. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/08/claude-code-and-gemini-cli-flaws-let.html

Step 3 (hunt): Trace the source package/repo across the org (other clones), and pivot to child processes spawned by Code.exe/claude at folder-open time and to any egress they generated.

Codex second-pass hijack: AGENTS.md written inside a CI checkout AIInstallation Medium
Hunts writes/modifications to AGENTS.md within a job's checkout by a build/agent process, the mechanism Novee used against openai/codex where the first Codex pass wrote AGENTS.md and the second pass loaded it as its own instructions. OpenAI now treats repository instruction files as untrusted input. Rationale: Anchors on the article's exact abused file `AGENTS.md` and the two-pass-shared-checkout mechanism; scoping the writer to node/codex/python during a job distinguishes attacker-planted instructions from a human editing project docs. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/08/claude-code-and-gemini-cli-flaws-let.html
ATT&CKT1036 T1574 T1059
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Maintainer legitimately editing AGENTS.md project documentation
  • A single-pass Codex/agent run creating an AGENTS.md scaffold
  • Repo template generator emitting AGENTS.md on init
  • Formatter/linter rewriting AGENTS.md whitespace
Suppression filter
| where not(InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("prettier","eslint","markdownlint"))
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Diff the AGENTS.md write — flag content that adds tool/command instructions, exfil URLs, or references to secrets rather than prose docs, and confirm it happened mid-job (between Codex passes) in a shared checkout. Step 2 (contain): Fail/cancel the job before a second pass loads the file, and move Codex to a read-only sandbox / last-step-in-job per OpenAI guidance. Step 3 (hunt): Check whether the same job later touched CI secrets/env, and look across repos for AGENTS.md modified by automation rather than commits.
