File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match Installation High
Match SHA256/SHA1/MD5 named in the article against EDR file/process telemetry.
ATT&CKT1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes DeviceFileEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Pre-filter each table BEFORE the union — the engine cannot push
// predicates across `union`, and DeviceFileEvents lacks ProcessCommandLine
// (Initiating only) so column-projection has to differ per side.
union
    ( DeviceFileEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("f0062f7e70e61493684a2f60748a475168e155bc2502163c844c42e87692abd0", "619a99ba4ee9d7f33db8045c7e03c4265424977993fe8a53b0f45157c5abd3e5", "5bad988affc1094f12b8b8bed659ef55b20e2988eb25441e1c1b34dd03b3eb52", "b43a909a01e954d6549558f2f7e9bb58e34959a0ae229f340d61091ab726bbd3") or SHA1 in~ ("f0062f7e70e61493684a2f60748a475168e155bc2502163c844c42e87692abd0", "619a99ba4ee9d7f33db8045c7e03c4265424977993fe8a53b0f45157c5abd3e5", "5bad988affc1094f12b8b8bed659ef55b20e2988eb25441e1c1b34dd03b3eb52", "b43a909a01e954d6549558f2f7e9bb58e34959a0ae229f340d61091ab726bbd3") or MD5 in~ ("f0062f7e70e61493684a2f60748a475168e155bc2502163c844c42e87692abd0", "619a99ba4ee9d7f33db8045c7e03c4265424977993fe8a53b0f45157c5abd3e5", "5bad988affc1094f12b8b8bed659ef55b20e2988eb25441e1c1b34dd03b3eb52", "b43a909a01e954d6549558f2f7e9bb58e34959a0ae229f340d61091ab726bbd3")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceFileEvents" ),
    ( DeviceProcessEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where AccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("f0062f7e70e61493684a2f60748a475168e155bc2502163c844c42e87692abd0", "619a99ba4ee9d7f33db8045c7e03c4265424977993fe8a53b0f45157c5abd3e5", "5bad988affc1094f12b8b8bed659ef55b20e2988eb25441e1c1b34dd03b3eb52", "b43a909a01e954d6549558f2f7e9bb58e34959a0ae229f340d61091ab726bbd3") or SHA1 in~ ("f0062f7e70e61493684a2f60748a475168e155bc2502163c844c42e87692abd0", "619a99ba4ee9d7f33db8045c7e03c4265424977993fe8a53b0f45157c5abd3e5", "5bad988affc1094f12b8b8bed659ef55b20e2988eb25441e1c1b34dd03b3eb52", "b43a909a01e954d6549558f2f7e9bb58e34959a0ae229f340d61091ab726bbd3") or MD5 in~ ("f0062f7e70e61493684a2f60748a475168e155bc2502163c844c42e87692abd0", "619a99ba4ee9d7f33db8045c7e03c4265424977993fe8a53b0f45157c5abd3e5", "5bad988affc1094f12b8b8bed659ef55b20e2988eb25441e1c1b34dd03b3eb52", "b43a909a01e954d6549558f2f7e9bb58e34959a0ae229f340d61091ab726bbd3")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = ProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceProcessEvents" )
| order by Timestamp desc

// Pre-filter both ASIM tables before the union — same pattern as the
// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["f0062f7e70e61493684a2f60748a475168e155bc2502163c844c42e87692abd0", "619a99ba4ee9d7f33db8045c7e03c4265424977993fe8a53b0f45157c5abd3e5", "5bad988affc1094f12b8b8bed659ef55b20e2988eb25441e1c1b34dd03b3eb52", "b43a909a01e954d6549558f2f7e9bb58e34959a0ae229f340d61091ab726bbd3"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha) · PowerShell encoded / obfuscated command · Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children · Article-specific behavioural hunt — ChainDrop: Inside a Self-Propagating npm Worm
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs

C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.

| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp

title: Infostealer - Non-Browser Process Accessing Browser Credential Stores
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d01
status: experimental
description: |
    Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies
    SQLite databases from Chrome/Edge/Firefox profile directories. Any
    non-browser process touching these files is a high-fidelity signal.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1539/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1555/003/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1539
    - attack.t1555.003
    - attack.credential-access
logsource:
    category: file_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_path:
        TargetFilename|contains:
            - '\Google\Chrome\User Data\'
            - '\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\'
            - '\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\'
    selection_file:
        TargetFilename|endswith:
            - '\Login Data'
            - '\Cookies'
            - '\logins.json'
            - '\cookies.sqlite'
    filter_browser:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\chrome.exe'
            - '\msedge.exe'
            - '\firefox.exe'
            - '\brave.exe'
            - '\opera.exe'
    condition: selection_path and selection_file and not filter_browser
falsepositives:
    - Backup utilities reading user profile files
    - Browser sync agents from non-stock vendors
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

title: FakeCaptcha / ClickFix - Clipboard-Injected PowerShell from Explorer
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d06
status: experimental
description: |
    "FakeCaptcha" / "ClickFix" social-engineering: malicious site asks
    user to press Win+R and paste a payload. The result is
    powershell/mshta launched directly from explorer.exe with iex /
    base64 / downloadstring in the command line.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/001/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1204/002/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1059.001
    - attack.t1204.002
    - attack.execution
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_parent:
        ParentImage|endswith:
            - '\explorer.exe'
            - '\RuntimeBroker.exe'
    selection_child:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\powershell.exe'
            - '\pwsh.exe'
            - '\mshta.exe'
    selection_cmd:
        CommandLine|contains:
            - 'iex'
            - 'invoke-expression'
            - 'frombase64'
            - 'downloadstring'
            - 'hxxp'
            - 'curl '
            - 'wget '
    condition: selection_parent and selection_child and selection_cmd
falsepositives:
    - IT-driven scripted automation that admins paste-launch
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("explorer.exe","RuntimeBroker.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","mshta.exe")
      AND (Processes.process="*iex*" OR Processes.process="*Invoke-Expression*"
        OR Processes.process="*FromBase64*" OR Processes.process="*DownloadString*"
        OR Processes.process="*hxxp*" OR Processes.process="*curl*" OR Processes.process="*wget*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("explorer.exe","RuntimeBroker.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","mshta.exe")
      AND (Processes.process="*iex*" OR Processes.process="*Invoke-Expression*"
        OR Processes.process="*FromBase64*" OR Processes.process="*DownloadString*"
        OR Processes.process="*hxxp*" OR Processes.process="*curl*" OR Processes.process="*wget*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`

File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match Installation High
Match SHA256/SHA1/MD5 named in the article against EDR file/process telemetry.
ATT&CKT1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes DeviceFileEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Pre-filter each table BEFORE the union — the engine cannot push
// predicates across `union`, and DeviceFileEvents lacks ProcessCommandLine
// (Initiating only) so column-projection has to differ per side.
union
    ( DeviceFileEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("d30b4ea6f68456672f5abb35e9dcf7d54226372b66e9d60a7ee26b7a52568e74", "9fc2570b7cef51c1b8df116d144d11ff4096357be7d2c4c6367cfc2509cf1bcc", "54dc7ea54a1317cca0e890a2770630cf7fa6c97813e0cb9d2caa93012b350668", "fd3ca4007b225fdf8de7af4345a19179d5efa8c4bb9205f88cda806e5684b1eb", "b27b82afa5f15512f3856e549fb83d873fd0049759a4b62ce64c8d7d4dc2c678") or SHA1 in~ ("d30b4ea6f68456672f5abb35e9dcf7d54226372b66e9d60a7ee26b7a52568e74", "9fc2570b7cef51c1b8df116d144d11ff4096357be7d2c4c6367cfc2509cf1bcc", "54dc7ea54a1317cca0e890a2770630cf7fa6c97813e0cb9d2caa93012b350668", "fd3ca4007b225fdf8de7af4345a19179d5efa8c4bb9205f88cda806e5684b1eb", "b27b82afa5f15512f3856e549fb83d873fd0049759a4b62ce64c8d7d4dc2c678") or MD5 in~ ("d30b4ea6f68456672f5abb35e9dcf7d54226372b66e9d60a7ee26b7a52568e74", "9fc2570b7cef51c1b8df116d144d11ff4096357be7d2c4c6367cfc2509cf1bcc", "54dc7ea54a1317cca0e890a2770630cf7fa6c97813e0cb9d2caa93012b350668", "fd3ca4007b225fdf8de7af4345a19179d5efa8c4bb9205f88cda806e5684b1eb", "b27b82afa5f15512f3856e549fb83d873fd0049759a4b62ce64c8d7d4dc2c678")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceFileEvents" ),
    ( DeviceProcessEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where AccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("d30b4ea6f68456672f5abb35e9dcf7d54226372b66e9d60a7ee26b7a52568e74", "9fc2570b7cef51c1b8df116d144d11ff4096357be7d2c4c6367cfc2509cf1bcc", "54dc7ea54a1317cca0e890a2770630cf7fa6c97813e0cb9d2caa93012b350668", "fd3ca4007b225fdf8de7af4345a19179d5efa8c4bb9205f88cda806e5684b1eb", "b27b82afa5f15512f3856e549fb83d873fd0049759a4b62ce64c8d7d4dc2c678") or SHA1 in~ ("d30b4ea6f68456672f5abb35e9dcf7d54226372b66e9d60a7ee26b7a52568e74", "9fc2570b7cef51c1b8df116d144d11ff4096357be7d2c4c6367cfc2509cf1bcc", "54dc7ea54a1317cca0e890a2770630cf7fa6c97813e0cb9d2caa93012b350668", "fd3ca4007b225fdf8de7af4345a19179d5efa8c4bb9205f88cda806e5684b1eb", "b27b82afa5f15512f3856e549fb83d873fd0049759a4b62ce64c8d7d4dc2c678") or MD5 in~ ("d30b4ea6f68456672f5abb35e9dcf7d54226372b66e9d60a7ee26b7a52568e74", "9fc2570b7cef51c1b8df116d144d11ff4096357be7d2c4c6367cfc2509cf1bcc", "54dc7ea54a1317cca0e890a2770630cf7fa6c97813e0cb9d2caa93012b350668", "fd3ca4007b225fdf8de7af4345a19179d5efa8c4bb9205f88cda806e5684b1eb", "b27b82afa5f15512f3856e549fb83d873fd0049759a4b62ce64c8d7d4dc2c678")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = ProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceProcessEvents" )
| order by Timestamp desc

// Pre-filter both ASIM tables before the union — same pattern as the
// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["d30b4ea6f68456672f5abb35e9dcf7d54226372b66e9d60a7ee26b7a52568e74", "9fc2570b7cef51c1b8df116d144d11ff4096357be7d2c4c6367cfc2509cf1bcc", "54dc7ea54a1317cca0e890a2770630cf7fa6c97813e0cb9d2caa93012b350668", "fd3ca4007b225fdf8de7af4345a19179d5efa8c4bb9205f88cda806e5684b1eb", "b27b82afa5f15512f3856e549fb83d873fd0049759a4b62ce64c8d7d4dc2c678"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] UNC6671 passkey/Okta AitM phishing domain & proxy IP callout · Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] Entra/Okta SSO sign-in from UNC6671 AitM reverse-proxy IPs · Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key.
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] Rapid multi-cloud app fan-out after single SSO sign-in (dashboard enumeration) · [LLM] Bulk deletion of security/password-reset/MFA emails post-SSO-compromise · [LLM] Automated bulk cloud data harvesting from compromised SSO session · Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs
UNC6671 passkey/Okta AitM phishing domain & proxy IP callout AIDelivery Medium
Hunts endpoint/proxy connections to the specific adversary-in-the-middle credential-harvesting domains and reverse-proxy IPs UNC6671 (BlackFile) uses in its help-desk vishing campaign against financial firms. High-fidelity because these are named, second-source-confirmed IOCs, not a generic lookalike heuristic. Rationale: Uses the 20 named passkey/Okta AitM domains and 11 reverse-proxy IPs from the article, cross-confirmed against GTIG's UNC6671 blog and Okta Threat Intelligence (myoktasso.com, setupssopasskey.com, passkeydeploy.com appear in both). Direct IOC match = very high fidelity. Cross-checked against: • https://cloud.google.com/blog/topics/threat-intelligence/unc6671-targets-financial-services-and-enterprise-cloud-environments • https://www.okta.com/blog/threat-intelligence/vishing-actors-target-microsoft-entra-passkey-enrollment-/
ATT&CKT1566.004 T1598.004 T1557
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic Web.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Security researcher or SOC analyst sandboxing the phishing URLs for triage
  • Threat-intel platform (e.g. urlscan.io agent) auto-detonating the domain from a corporate egress IP
  • DNS sinkhole / secure web gateway that resolves-then-blocks logging the lookup
  • User forwarded the vishing SMS link and clicked to report it via a phish-report button
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe") and InitiatingProcessAccountName in~ ("soc-analyst","threatintel-svc"))
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Identify the user/device behind the connection; confirm whether creds/session were entered (check timestamp vs. subsequent SigninLogs). Pull the full URL path for the impersonated brand. 2) CONTAIN: Immediately revoke all refresh/session tokens for the user (Entra 'Revoke Sessions' / Okta clear sessions), force password + passkey re-enrollment, and block the domains/IPs at proxy and DNS. 3) HUNT: Pivot on the account into UC 'multi-cloud enumeration', UC 'security-email deletion', and UC 'bulk download' to determine if the AitM cookie was replayed and data accessed.

Entra/Okta SSO sign-in from UNC6671 AitM reverse-proxy IPs AIExploitation Medium
Detects successful or attempted cloud SSO authentication originating from the specific reverse-proxy IPs UNC6671 uses to relay stolen credentials and replay intercepted session cookies against Microsoft 365 / Okta. Fires on the moment the attacker rides the AitM-stolen session into the tenant. Rationale: Anchors on the 11 article-provided AitM proxy IPs cross-confirmed by GTIG. Any tenant sign-in from these IPs indicates the attacker is riding the stolen SSO session — near-zero legitimate reason for a corporate identity to authenticate from this infrastructure. Falcon left empty: Entra/Okta sign-in telemetry is not in FDR endpoint data. Cross-checked against: • https://cloud.google.com/blog/topics/threat-intelligence/unc6671-targets-financial-services-and-enterprise-cloud-environments • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/hedge-fund-cyberattacks-tied-to-blackfile-linked-unc6671-extortion-group/
ATT&CKT1078.004 T1539 T1557
Data sourcesAuthentication.Authentication
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A traveling employee behind the same shared hosting/VPN egress range (rare for these bulletproof ranges)
  • SOC-controlled breach-and-attack-simulation replaying the IOC set against a test account
  • Threat-intel enrichment service that authenticates test creds to validate the phishing kit
  • IP re-assigned by the hosting provider to a benign tenant after takedown (validate recency of IOC)
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Confirm ResultType==0 (successful) vs failure; if successful, treat account as compromised. Compare UserAgent/ClientAppUsed to the user's known baseline and check ConditionalAccessStatus. 2) CONTAIN: Revoke sessions and refresh tokens, disable the account or force re-auth with a phishing-resistant method, and add the IPs to a named-location block in Conditional Access. 3) HUNT: Enumerate all resources the token touched (chain to multi-cloud enumeration UC) and review mailbox rules + deletions for cover-up activity.
let PhishIPs = dynamic(["31.7.56.61","31.7.56.52","193.34.212.132","185.178.208.153","23.234.75.84","195.140.213.114","195.140.213.115","107.128.45.122","76.103.148.180","38.42.59.171","47.218.103.146"]);
AADSignInEventsBeta
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where IPAddress in (PhishIPs)
| project Timestamp, AccountUpn, AccountDisplayName, Application, ApplicationId, IPAddress, Country, City, ClientAppUsed, ErrorCode, RiskLevelDuringSignIn, ConditionalAccessStatus, UserAgent, IsInteractive
| order by Timestamp desc

| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)

| project TimeGenerated, UserPrincipalName, UserDisplayName, AppDisplayName, IPAddress, Location, ClientAppUsed, ResultType, RiskLevelDuringSignIn, ConditionalAccessStatus, UserAgent

Rapid multi-cloud app fan-out after single SSO sign-in (dashboard enumeration) AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts the UNC6671 post-compromise behaviour where operators log into the SSO dashboard and immediately pivot into every linked cloud platform. Flags a single identity authenticating to an abnormal number of distinct cloud resources inside a tight window — the signature of automated SSO-dashboard harvesting. Rationale: Directly models the article's statement that after stealing M365/Okta SSO, attackers 'log into the SSO dashboard, which gives access to all the cloud platforms linked to the account.' The dcount-of-distinct-resources-in-a-window pivot targets the automated fan-out rather than any single sign-in. Threshold (>=5/10m) is a hunting starting point to be tuned per tenant baseline. Cross-checked against: • https://cloud.google.com/blog/topics/threat-intelligence/unc6671-targets-financial-services-and-enterprise-cloud-environments • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/hedge-fund-cyberattacks-tied-to-blackfile-linked-unc6671-extortion-group/
ATT&CKT1078.004 T1526
Data sourcesAuthentication.Authentication
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Power user or executive legitimately opening many SSO tiles at start of day
  • Automated SSO app provisioning / SCIM sync run under a user context
  • New-hire onboarding where many apps are accessed for first-time setup
  • Conditional Access token broker generating multiple resource sign-ins from one interactive auth
  • Mobile device app refresh issuing sign-ins to many resources near-simultaneously
Suppression filter
| where AccountUpn !endswith "$" and IPs !has "corporate-egress-range" | where not (Apps has "Microsoft App Access Panel" and DistinctApps < 8)
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Rank the flagged sessions by novelty — cross-check the source IP against UC 'AitM proxy IP' and whether the resource set differs from the user's 30-day baseline. Non-business-hours + new IP = escalate. 2) CONTAIN: If confirmed, revoke tokens and quarantine the account; snapshot which apps were reached to scope the blast radius. 3) HUNT: For each app touched (SharePoint/OneDrive/Salesforce/etc.), pivot to the bulk-download UC and review for data export and mailbox rule/deletion tampering.
AADSignInEventsBeta
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ErrorCode == 0
| summarize DistinctApps = dcount(ResourceDisplayName), Apps = make_set(ResourceDisplayName, 50), IPs = make_set(IPAddress, 10), FirstSeen = min(Timestamp), LastSeen = max(Timestamp) by AccountUpn, bin(Timestamp, 10m)
| where DistinctApps >= 5   // 5+ distinct cloud resources authenticated in 10 min = SSO-dashboard fan-out (human baseline P99 ~ 3)
| order by DistinctApps desc
SigninLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ResultType == 0
| summarize DistinctApps = dcount(ResourceDisplayName), Apps = make_set(ResourceDisplayName, 50), IPs = make_set(IPAddress, 10), FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated) by UserPrincipalName, bin(TimeGenerated, 10m)
| where DistinctApps >= 5   // 5+ distinct cloud resources in 10 min = SSO-dashboard fan-out
| order by DistinctApps desc

Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.

Bulk deletion of security/password-reset/MFA emails post-SSO-compromise AIActions on Objectives Medium
Detects the UNC6671 cover-up step where operators delete security notifications and password-reset emails from a compromised inbox to hide the intrusion. Correlates mailbox delete operations targeting security-themed subjects within a tight window — a deliberate trace-erasure pattern distinct from normal user cleanup. Rationale: Implements the article's explicit claim that attackers 'delete security notifications and password-reset emails from compromised inboxes.' The subject-keyword filter plus a per-window count isolates targeted trace-erasure from random cleanup. Datadog/Falcon/CloudWatch left empty: O365 mailbox-audit telemetry is not in those pipelines here. Cross-checked against: • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/hedge-fund-cyberattacks-tied-to-blackfile-linked-unc6671-extortion-group/ • https://cloud.google.com/blog/topics/threat-intelligence/unc6671-targets-financial-services-and-enterprise-cloud-environments
ATT&CKT1070.008 T1114
Data sources
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • User bulk-clearing a noisy 'security alert' newsletter or automated report folder
  • Inbox rule auto-deleting recurring MFA/verification emails the user set up
  • Mailbox retention/DLP policy purging aged items in a batch
  • Help-desk-assisted mailbox cleanup during legitimate account maintenance
  • Shared mailbox where multiple users triage and delete alert mail
Suppression filter
| where DeletedCount >= 3 and Subjects has_any ("password reset","passkey","unusual sign-in") | where not (IPAddress in ("corporate-egress-range"))
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Confirm the deletions cluster in time and correlate the ClientIP with UC 'AitM proxy IP' or an anomalous SSO sign-in; recover deleted items from Recoverable Items to read what was hidden. 2) CONTAIN: Revoke sessions, reset creds + passkey, enable mailbox litigation hold to stop further purging, and check for attacker-created inbox rules. 3) HUNT: Look for the password-reset/MFA events that generated the deleted mail (AuditLogs) to find which downstream accounts the attacker was resetting; pivot to bulk-download UC.
CloudAppEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where Application == "Microsoft Exchange Online"
| where ActionType in ("SoftDelete","HardDelete","MoveToDeletedItems","Delete")
| extend Subject = tostring(RawEventData.Item.Subject)
| where Subject has_any ("password","passkey","MFA","multi-factor","verification code","security alert","sign-in","unusual","reset","authenticator")
| summarize DeletedCount = count(), Subjects = make_set(Subject, 20), FirstSeen = min(Timestamp), LastSeen = max(Timestamp) by AccountObjectId, AccountDisplayName, IPAddress, bin(Timestamp, 15m)
| where DeletedCount >= 3   // 3+ security-themed mail deletions in 15 min = deliberate trace erasure
| order by DeletedCount desc
OfficeActivity
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
| where Operation in ("SoftDelete","HardDelete","MoveToDeletedItems")
| where Subject has_any ("password","passkey","MFA","multi-factor","verification code","security alert","sign-in","unusual","reset","authenticator")
| summarize DeletedCount = count(), Subjects = make_set(Subject, 20), FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated) by UserId, ClientIP, bin(TimeGenerated, 15m)
| where DeletedCount >= 3   // 3+ security-themed mail deletions in 15 min = deliberate trace erasure
| order by DeletedCount desc
CLOUD
`o365_management_activity` Workload=Exchange Operation IN ("SoftDelete","HardDelete","MoveToDeletedItems") (Item.Subject="*password*" OR Item.Subject="*passkey*" OR Item.Subject="*MFA*" OR Item.Subject="*multi-factor*" OR Item.Subject="*verification code*" OR Item.Subject="*security alert*" OR Item.Subject="*sign-in*" OR Item.Subject="*unusual*" OR Item.Subject="*reset*" OR Item.Subject="*authenticator*") | bin _time span=15m | stats count as DeletedCount values(Item.Subject) as Subjects values(ClientIP) as ClientIP by UserId _time | where DeletedCount >= 3 | sort - DeletedCount
Automated bulk cloud data harvesting from compromised SSO session AIActions on Objectives Medium
Detects the UNC6671 collection/exfil stage where automated Python/PowerShell tooling recursively downloads data from every reachable cloud service (SharePoint/OneDrive/Teams) after SSO takeover. Flags a single identity performing an abnormal volume of file downloads in a short window — the non-human harvesting signature. Rationale: Models the article's line that attackers 'use automated tools to steal data from all cloud services they gain access to' (GTIG attributes Python/PowerShell exfil scripts). The high-volume, short-window download count with a UserAgent pivot isolates scripted harvesting from human browsing. Threshold is a hunting seed to tune against tenant baselines. Cross-checked against: • https://cloud.google.com/blog/topics/threat-intelligence/unc6671-targets-financial-services-and-enterprise-cloud-environments • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/hedge-fund-cyberattacks-tied-to-blackfile-linked-unc6671-extortion-group/
ATT&CKT1537 T1530
Data sources
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate OneDrive/SharePoint full-sync on a new device or after a client reset
  • eDiscovery / legal-hold export job run under a user context
  • Data-migration or backup tooling (e.g. tenant-to-tenant migration) authenticated as a user
  • Analyst pulling a large research dataset for a legitimate project
  • Automated reporting bot with delegated access reading many files
Suppression filter
| where UserAgent has_any ("python","powershell","curl","axios","Go-http-client") or DownloadCount >= 250 | where not (Apps has "Microsoft SkyDriveSync" and DownloadCount < 300)
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Inspect UserAgent for scripting stacks (python-requests, PowerShell, curl) and correlate ClientIP against UC 'AitM proxy IP'; a non-browser UserAgent + new IP is high-signal. 2) CONTAIN: Revoke tokens, suspend the account, and apply a sensitivity-label/DLP block on the affected sites to halt further pulls. 3) HUNT: Enumerate exactly which files/sites were downloaded to scope data loss for extortion notification, check for outbound transfer to attacker cloud accounts, and confirm mailbox trace-erasure (deletion UC).
CloudAppEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ActionType in ("FileDownloaded","FileSyncDownloadedFull","FileAccessed","FilePreviewed")
| summarize DownloadCount = count(), DistinctFiles = dcount(ObjectName), Apps = make_set(Application, 10), FirstSeen = min(Timestamp), LastSeen = max(Timestamp) by AccountObjectId, AccountDisplayName, IPAddress, UserAgent, bin(Timestamp, 10m)
| where DownloadCount >= 100   // 100+ downloads in 10 min = automated harvesting (human P99 ~ dozens)
| order by DownloadCount desc
OfficeActivity
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where Operation in ("FileDownloaded","FileSyncDownloadedFull","FileAccessed")
| summarize DownloadCount = count(), DistinctFiles = dcount(SourceFileName), FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated) by UserId, ClientIP, UserAgent, bin(TimeGenerated, 10m)
| where DownloadCount >= 100   // 100+ downloads in 10 min = automated harvesting
| order by DownloadCount desc
ENDPOINT
`o365_management_activity` Operation IN ("FileDownloaded","FileSyncDownloadedFull","FileAccessed") | bin _time span=10m | stats count as DownloadCount dc(SourceFileName) as DistinctFiles values(ClientIP) as ClientIP values(UserAgent) as UserAgent by UserId _time | where DownloadCount >= 100 | sort - DownloadCount
Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs Actions on Objectives High
Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies SQLite from Chrome/Edge/Firefox.

Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where FolderPath has_any (@"\Google\Chrome\User Data\", @"\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\", @"\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\")
| where FileName in~ ("Login Data","Cookies","logins.json","cookies.sqlite")

// ASIM ImFileEvent — covers MDE, Sysmon, AuditD, Defender for Cloud, etc.
ImFileEvent

| where TargetFilePath has_any (@"\Google\Chrome\User Data\",

title: Infostealer - Non-Browser Process Accessing Browser Credential Stores
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d01
status: experimental
description: |
    Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies
    SQLite databases from Chrome/Edge/Firefox profile directories. Any
    non-browser process touching these files is a high-fidelity signal.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1539/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1555/003/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1539
    - attack.t1555.003
    - attack.credential-access
logsource:
    category: file_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_path:
        TargetFilename|contains:
            - '\Google\Chrome\User Data\'
            - '\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\'
            - '\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\'
    selection_file:
        TargetFilename|endswith:
            - '\Login Data'
            - '\Cookies'
            - '\logins.json'
            - '\cookies.sqlite'
    filter_browser:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\chrome.exe'
            - '\msedge.exe'
            - '\firefox.exe'
            - '\brave.exe'
            - '\opera.exe'
    condition: selection_path and selection_file and not filter_browser
falsepositives:
    - Backup utilities reading user profile files
    - Browser sync agents from non-stock vendors
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```

    from datamodel=Web

| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`

    [| tstats summariesonly=false count

     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count
    from datamodel=Email.All_Email
    where All_Email.file_name!="-"
    by All_Email.src_user, All_Email.recipient, All_Email.file_name, All_Email.subject
| rename All_Email.recipient as user

    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
        from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes

          AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
        by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process

    [| tstats summariesonly=false count

Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process Exploitation High

Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration. → Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s)
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] Anomalous POST to SharePoint ToolPane/_trust exploit endpoints (CVE-2026-50522/56164)
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] SharePoint IIS worker (w3wp.exe) spawning command interpreter — ToolShell RCE
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] SharePoint MachineKey / web.config credential theft via w3wp child process · [LLM] Webshell/.aspx written into SharePoint LAYOUTS by w3wp.exe (ToolShell persistence)
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change · LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) · Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement
Anomalous POST to SharePoint ToolPane/_trust exploit endpoints (CVE-2026-50522/56164) AIDelivery Medium
Hunts inbound POST requests to the SharePoint endpoints abused by the July 2026 patch-Tuesday chain — /_layouts/15/ToolPane.aspx and the /_trust/default.aspx WS-Federation sign-in path where CVE-2026-50522 delivers a BinaryFormatter SecurityContextToken cookie. Surfaces the first foothold on internet-facing SharePoint servers. Rationale: Uses the two concrete exploit endpoints corroborated for this chain — ToolPane.aspx (CVE-2026-56164 EoP path) and /_trust/default.aspx (CVE-2026-50522 WS-Federation deserialization). Referer and low status codes help separate exploit probes from legit editing. Cross-checked against: • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/critical-sharepoint-rce-flaw-exploited-to-steal-machine-keys/ • https://www.helpnetsecurity.com/2026/07/22/sharepoint-cve-2026-50522-exploited/ • https://www.trellix.com/blogs/research/toolshell-unleashed-decoding-the-sharepoint-attack-chain/
ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesWeb.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate SharePoint page authors editing web-part zones hit ToolPane.aspx from internal IPs
  • Federated SSO / ADFS traffic legitimately posting to /_trust/default.aspx
  • Vulnerability scanners (Qualys/Tenable) probing SharePoint endpoints
  • Load-balancer / uptime monitors POSTing health checks
  • SharePoint farm timer jobs generating internal POSTs
Suppression filter
| where NOT (cidr_match("10.0.0.0/8", cIP) OR cidr_match("192.168.0.0/16", cIP))
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the cIP is external/untrusted and correlate the timestamp with w3wp.exe child-process activity (UC2) on the same Computer. Pull the full csUriQuery and User-Agent. 2) Contain: block external access to SharePoint (as BIT did), and firewall the source IP; snapshot the server for forensics. 3) Hunt: pivot to any w3wp.exe→cmd/powershell spawns, reads of web.config/machine.config, and newly written .aspx files under the LAYOUTS directory in the following hours.
W3CIISLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where csMethod == "POST"
| where csUriStem has_any ("/_layouts/15/ToolPane.aspx", "/_trust/default.aspx") or csUriStem endswith "ToolPane.aspx"
| where scStatus in ("200","302","401","500")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, cIP, csMethod, csUriStem, csUriQuery, csReferer, scStatus, csUserAgent
| order by TimeGenerated desc

SharePoint IIS worker (w3wp.exe) spawning command interpreter — ToolShell RCE AIExploitation High
Alerts when the SharePoint/IIS worker process w3wp.exe spawns cmd.exe, powershell.exe or other interpreters/LOLBins. This parent→child chain is the execution signature of CVE-2026-50522 RCE and does not occur in normal SharePoint operation. Rationale: w3wp.exe (SharePoint app-pool worker) spawning an interpreter is the highest-fidelity execution signal for this chain — corroborated across Splunk, Trellix and Anomali ToolShell writeups as abnormal in legitimate SharePoint operation. Named parent/child binaries make it alert-grade. Cross-checked against: • https://www.splunk.com/en_us/blog/security/sharepoint-exploits-and-the-hidden-threat-of-iis-module-persistence.html • https://www.anomali.com/blog/detecting-the-toolshell-sharepoint-exploit • https://www.trellix.com/blogs/research/toolshell-unleashed-decoding-the-sharepoint-attack-chain/
ATT&CKT1190 T1059.001 T1059.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • SharePoint installation/patching (PSConfig) transiently running under an app-pool identity
  • Admin-authored SharePoint timer jobs or custom web parts shelling out
  • Health-analyzer or monitoring solutions invoking scripts via the worker process
  • Antivirus/EDR remediation spawning under w3wp context
  • Custom in-house SharePoint solutions that legitimately call certutil/PowerShell
Suppression filter
| where not (ProcessCommandLine has_any ("PSConfig","wsadmin","stsadm") and InitiatingProcessIntegrityLevel == "System")
Response runbook
1) Triage: capture the child ProcessCommandLine — decode any -EncodedCommand, look for download/machine-key strings. Correlate with UC1 inbound POSTs on the same host/time. 2) Contain: isolate the SharePoint server from the network and block external SharePoint access; suspend the app pool. Because machine keys may be stolen, plan key rotation + server reinstall (BIT reinstalled affected servers). 3) Hunt: search for web.config/machine.config reads (UC3), dropped .aspx webshells (UC4), and forged-token sign-ins across the ~200 potentially affected accounts.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "w3wp.exe"
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","mshta.exe","cscript.exe","wscript.exe","rundll32.exe","csc.exe","certutil.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessIntegrityLevel, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "\\w3wp.exe"
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\\cmd.exe","\\powershell.exe","\\pwsh.exe","\\mshta.exe","\\cscript.exe","\\wscript.exe","\\rundll32.exe","\\csc.exe","\\certutil.exe")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, ParentProcessName, NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

SharePoint MachineKey / web.config credential theft via w3wp child process AIInstallation High
Detects the credential-access step of CVE-2026-50522 where post-RCE code reads SharePoint ValidationKey/DecryptionKey material from web.config or machine.config to forge __VIEWSTATE/auth tokens. Fires on an interpreter spawned by w3wp.exe whose command line references machine-key config or key fields. Rationale: Targets the exact post-exploitation objective corroborated by BleepingComputer/HelpNetSecurity/watchTowr for CVE-2026-50522: stealing SharePoint machine keys (ValidationKey/DecryptionKey) from web.config/machine.config to forge tokens. The w3wp parent + key-material string combo is very high fidelity. Cross-checked against: • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/critical-sharepoint-rce-flaw-exploited-to-steal-machine-keys/ • https://www.helpnetsecurity.com/2026/07/22/sharepoint-cve-2026-50522-exploited/ • https://www.trellix.com/blogs/research/toolshell-unleashed-decoding-the-sharepoint-attack-chain/
ATT&CKT1552.004 T1552.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • SharePoint patch/config operations (PSConfig, Update-SPMachineKey) legitimately touching machine keys
  • Admin PowerShell reading web.config for troubleshooting under the app-pool account
  • Farm build automation that rotates machine keys
  • Backup jobs enumerating config files
  • Custom deployment scripts referencing web.config paths
Suppression filter
| where not (ProcessCommandLine has_any ("Update-SPMachineKey","PSConfig") and AccountName endswith "$")
Response runbook
1) Triage: capture the full command line and determine whether ValidationKey/DecryptionKey values were read or written out (base64/file redirection). Confirm the parent w3wp and any preceding UC1 POST. 2) Contain: treat machine keys as compromised — isolate the server, rotate/regenerate SharePoint machine keys across the farm, and force password resets on affected accounts (BIT reset ~200). 3) Hunt: because stolen keys enable forged tokens surviving patching, hunt for anomalous authenticated SharePoint sessions and __VIEWSTATE replays after the reset, and plan server reinstall.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "w3wp.exe"
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","cscript.exe","wscript.exe")
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("machineKey","ValidationKey","DecryptionKey","web.config","machine.config")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "\\w3wp.exe"
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\\powershell.exe","\\pwsh.exe","\\cmd.exe","\\cscript.exe","\\wscript.exe")
| where CommandLine has_any ("machineKey","ValidationKey","DecryptionKey","web.config","machine.config")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, ParentProcessName, NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Webshell/.aspx written into SharePoint LAYOUTS by w3wp.exe (ToolShell persistence) AIInstallation Medium
Detects the SharePoint worker process writing new .aspx/.ashx files into the SharePoint TEMPLATE\LAYOUTS or web-root directories — the webshell/key-exfil persistence pattern (e.g. spinstall0.aspx) used in the ToolShell chain to drop a page that returns the stolen machine keys or maintains RCE access. Rationale: The SharePoint worker writing a fresh .aspx into LAYOUTS (the spinstall0.aspx-style key-exfil/webshell drop documented in ToolShell) is a rare, high-signal persistence event that maps directly to this campaign's machine-key theft and post-patch access retention. Cross-checked against: • https://www.trellix.com/blogs/research/toolshell-unleashed-decoding-the-sharepoint-attack-chain/ • https://www.sygnia.co/threat-reports-and-advisories/on-prem-sharepoint-toolshell-backdoor-advisory/ • https://www.anomali.com/blog/detecting-the-toolshell-sharepoint-exploit
ATT&CKT1505.003 T1190
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • SharePoint patching/PSConfig deploying legitimate new LAYOUTS pages
  • Installation of a SharePoint solution package (WSP) that provisions .aspx files
  • Farm feature activation writing application pages
  • Third-party SharePoint add-in deployment
  • Developer publishing a custom application page during a maintenance window
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("PSConfig","stsadm","Install-SPSolution"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: retrieve and read the dropped .aspx — look for code that outputs ValidationKey/DecryptionKey, accepts commands, or reflects __VIEWSTATE. Note file hash and creation time; correlate with UC1/UC2/UC3. 2) Contain: remove/quarantine the file, isolate the server, and treat machine keys as stolen (rotate keys, reset affected account passwords, reinstall server per BIT's remediation). 3) Hunt: enumerate all recently-created .aspx/.ashx across the farm, check IIS logs for GETs to the dropped filename from external IPs, and review authenticated sessions for forged-token reuse post-patch.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ActionType == "FileCreated"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "w3wp.exe"
| where FileName endswith ".aspx" or FileName endswith ".ashx"
| where FolderPath has_any (@"\TEMPLATE\LAYOUTS", @"\16\TEMPLATE", @"\web server extensions", @"\wwwroot")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, FileName, FolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventType == "FileCreated"
| where ActingProcessName endswith "\\w3wp.exe"
| where TargetFileName endswith ".aspx" or TargetFileName endswith ".ashx"
| where TargetFilePath has_any ("\\TEMPLATE\\LAYOUTS", "\\16\\TEMPLATE", "\\web server extensions", "\\wwwroot")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents

| where Timestamp > ago(1d)

LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) Actions on Objectives High
Mimikatz, comsvcs.dll MiniDump, or any non-Windows process opening LSASS.
ATT&CKT1003.001 T1003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType == "OpenProcessApiCall"
| where FileName =~ "lsass.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe","csrss.exe",
                                          "svchost.exe","wininit.exe","services.exe",
                                          "lsm.exe","SearchProtocolHost.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFolderPath, AccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
// SecurityEvent EventID 4663 = object access. AccessMask 0x10 / 0x40 / 0x1010
// indicate read access to lsass.exe — credential-dump signature. Audit
// Object Access > Audit File System policy required.
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4663
| where ObjectName endswith "\lsass.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ObjectName, ProcessName,
          AccessMask, AccessReason
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children · Article-specific behavioural hunt — Why metaphor may dictate your security strategy
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage.
Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web

    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url

| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
